item.title: European Unrest Prompts Military Deployments; West Bank Violence Escalates: On Air, October 21, 2026
item.description:
French Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced new curfews would be imposed where necessary, with local authorities coordinating decisions. Targeted curfews helped maintain calm overnight into Tuesday, following days of widespread unrest. Police confirmed Monday night passed without major incidents across France, though more than 2,000 people were arrested during the weekend.
Israeli settlers burned a welcome sign at the entrance of Burqa, a village east of Ramallah in the occupied West Bank, on Tuesday. Sayel Kanaan, head of the Burqa council, stated settlers ignited vehicle tires on the sign's stonework. Israeli police detained 10 people in connection with West Bank settler attacks, which included an assault on US photojournalist Heidi Levine and European diplomats.
France will deploy military forces, specifically the Sentinelle force, during upcoming protests planned for Saturday, October 24. Interior Minister Laurent Nunez announced the deployment aims to free police and gendarmes for maintaining order. Prime Minister Lecornu stated police deployment for Saturday's demonstrations would be massive, seeking an immediate return to order.
French security forces arrested a man believed linked to ultra-left movements over the burning down of the Limoges town hall. Anti-terror police investigate the suspected arson of the 1883 building, whose roof and belfry collapsed on Saturday, October 17. The man was arrested by officers from the specialized RAID police unit in Val d’Issoire.
Italy's government deploys 500 army troops to Milan to bolster security following a weekend of riots, looting, and clashes. Deputy Prime Minister Matteo Salvini announced the troop deployment, stating it moved "from words to action." The unrest occurred during demonstrations against the rising cost of living and poor public services, leading to smashed windows and looted shops.
Sudan's Foreign Ministry summoned Ambassador Essam Mohamed Karrar to express strong objection to a drone strike in the Abyei region. Abyei's information minister, Yohana Akol Ngor, stated the Amiet Market was hit by several drones, including a fuel depot used by Sudan's paramilitary Rapid Support Forces. The UN spokesperson Stéphane Dujarric expressed alarm over continued deadly drone strikes across Sudan.
The US Homeland Security Department ordered civilian federal agencies to remove and stop acquiring products and services using China's DeepSeek AI model. The US government cited "multiple threat vectors" and concerns about sensitive data transfer to China due to DeepSeek's servers. China’s commerce ministry condemned the US order, calling for an immediate reversal of the restrictive measures.
The Department of Justice charged 28 individuals, including green card holders, with crimes related to voter fraud in California. Eleven of the accused were arrested as part of "Operation Protect the Vote." The DOJ stated all 28 are lawful permanent residents not permitted to vote, facing charges of unlawful voting and falsely claiming U.S. citizenship.
Christiane Amanpour, CNN's chief international anchor, will leave the network in June 2027 after 43 years. She announced her daily show "Amanpour" on CNN International will scale back to once a week in early 2027 and conclude in May. Amanpour, 68, plans to continue her podcast "The Ex Files" with her ex-husband, Jamie Rubin.
President Donald Trump renewed his call for New Mexico to change its name to "New America," stating on Truth Social, "We are not Mexico, we are the United States of America!" He claimed the name change would add great value and prestige to the State and boost residents' pride.
Full bias analysis and source spectrum: https://news.voidvision.org/onair/.

item.title: France Orders Curfews Amid Widespread Unrest, Yemen Strike Kills Dozens: On Air, October 19, 2026
item.description:
Localized curfews begin Monday evening in several French cities, including Lille, Douai, and Wattigni, following widespread rioting and looting over the weekend. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu announced the partial measures, stating they were better adapted than a nationwide state of emergency, which he did not rule out if violence continued. President Emmanuel Macron refused Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez's offer to resign, instructing him to address security failures.
Protesters blocked the entrance to the Louvre in Paris on Monday, fueled by grievances over the cost of living, inflation, education conditions, and declining public services.
Iran-backed Houthi rebels struck Yemeni government forces with ballistic missiles on Monday, killing at least 53 soldiers at the al-Alam military camp in Shabwa province. The attack wounded an additional 200 recruits. Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree confirmed the group targeted the camp, claiming it was run by Saudi forces. The provincial government in Shabwa stated the death toll is preliminary and may rise.
Trump stated that if Israel chooses a leader other than Netanyahu, the United States would have to confront Iran alone, a task he is not inclined to undertake. Netanyahu thanked Trump for his support, pledging to "complete the mission" together.
Independent MP Helen Haines remains in critical condition after being struck by a car outside her Wangaratta office on Monday afternoon. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese described the incident as an "apparent attack" and a "deliberate act," not an accident. Victoria Police activated the Joint Counter Terrorism Team, which includes the Australian Federal Police, Victoria Police, and ASIO, to investigate the incident. A 43-year-old man was arrested at the scene, and a knife was seized from inside the vehicle.
A Kenyan court convicted self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie and 28 associates of murdering 191 people, including 190 children, in the Shakahola starvation cult case. The court rejected the defense's argument that the victims voluntarily fasted to death. Hundreds of bodies, totaling over 400, have been recovered from the Shakahola Forest since 2023. Post-mortems indicated many victims died from starvation, but also from asphyxia, neck compression, and traumatic head injuries.
The US Supreme Court on Monday rejected an appeal by Khalid Sheikh Mohammed, the accused mastermind of the September 11, 2001, attacks, and two co-defendants to revive a 2024 plea deal. The agreement would have spared Mohammed, Mustafa al Hawsawi, and Walid bin 'Atash the death penalty in exchange for guilty pleas. Former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin revoked the plea deals in 2024, two days after they were offered and accepted.
The Supreme Court agreed on Monday to review a Reconstruction-era ban on distilling spirits in private homes. The court will consider whether Congress had the constitutional authority to impose the 1868 ban. Federal law makes home distilling a crime punishable by up to five years in prison and a $10,000 fine, with violators' homes and property also subject to forfeiture. The government collected $11.1 billion in alcohol taxes in fiscal year 2023, with $6.8 billion from distilled spirits.
Former President Barack Obama on Sunday called the federal criminal investigation into Representative Ilhan Omar "appalling," stating the Trump administration is bringing the full weight of the federal government against an elected official for criticizing the president. Federal agents raided Omar's Washington, D.C., home as part of the investigation into her immigration status.
